text: A Weekly Dispatch for the Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist The Ether Gazette “Vigilance, distilled.” Week of August 3, 2026 Vol. 1, No. 6 Est. 2026 📰 Headlines A Federal Judge Blocks New Loan Limits for Nursing Students Days Before They Were Set to Take Effect On June 25, U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell issued a preliminary injunction blocking a Department of Education rule that would have redefined "professional degree" programs to exclude nursing — including nurse anesthesia — from the higher federal loan limits available to law, medicine, and other professional-track students. Filed by the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, the PA Education Association, and other trade groups, the suit argued the Department exceeded its statutory authority; Howell agreed the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits. Had the rule taken effect July 1 as scheduled, graduate nursing students — DNP and CRNA students among them — would have seen annual borrowing capped at $20,500 (aggregate $100,000), instead of the $50,000-per-year, $200,000-aggregate ceiling available to "professional degree" programs. The injunction runs alongside, but is separate from, the AANA-joined "Nurse-Forward" lawsuit filed May 29 challenging the same underlying rule; both cases continue while litigation plays out. ABC News · Nursing Gains 'Professional' Label for Student Loans After Judge's Ruling Sixth Circuit Rules AANA Lacks Standing to Challenge Insurers Over CRNA Reimbursement Rates On July 21, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled against AANA in its case seeking to compel HHS enforcement of the ACA's provider-nondiscrimination provision — the rule barring insurers from paying CRNAs less than physicians for identical services solely based on license type. The court didn't reach the merits of the discrimination claim; it held instead that AANA lacked associational standing to sue on its members' behalf. AANA President Jeff Molter was pointed in response: "This decision does not validate the behavior of insurance companies," he said, adding that below-parity reimbursement "remain[s] unlawful under current statute." With the federal appellate avenue narrowed, AANA says it will lean on state-level advocacy and look for other federal pathways to press the reimbursement fight. PR Newswire · Statement from AANA President Jeff Molter on the Sixth Circuit Decision Bipartisan Pushback Grows Against Medicare Contractors' Plan to Stop Covering Nerve Blocks for Chronic Pain Five Medicare Administrative Contractors have proposed local coverage determinations that would deny payment for peripheral nerve blocks used to treat chronic pain — procedures regional anesthesiologists and CRNAs perform routinely as an opioid-sparing alternative. A coalition led by ASA, ASRA Pain Medicine, IPSIS, and AAPM&R is fighting the proposals, and 25 bipartisan members of Congress, led by Reps. Brittany Pettersen and Claudia Tenney, wrote CMS warning that eliminating coverage "could result in a spike in opioid use and misuse." The proposed LCDs remain unfinalized; opponents are pushing for outright withdrawal rather than a narrowed version, arguing that even a scaled-back policy would strand patients who rely on nerve blocks as a non-opioid option. Becker's ASC · What Happened to the Nerve Block Coverage Denial? Where the Fight Stands Now Propofol Shortage Persists as Dr. Reddy's Exits the Market Dr. Reddy's Laboratories discontinued its propofol emulsion injection line in early 2026, according to its own SEC filings, deepening a shortage that has now stretched into its fourth year on the ASHP tracker. ASHP continues to list propofol as an active national shortage, and pharmacy leaders are advising anesthesia departments to keep contingency plans — etomidate, ketamine, or a volatile induction where appropriate — current rather than assuming steady vial availability through the fall. Event details at apsf.org → 📚 From the Literature The Study Behind the FDA's Sevoflurane Alert: How One Mitochondrial Variant Turns a Routine Anesthetic Catastrophic Following up on the FDA's July 2 alert (covered in our July 27 issue), the Anesthesiology paper behind it identifies a mechanism: patients carrying the mitochondrial DNA variant m.11232T>C — concentrated along a specific Venezuelan maternal lineage — carry a leucine-to-proline substitution in Complex I of the electron transport chain. In vitro, sevoflurane exposure in cells carrying the variant sharply suppressed mitochondrial oxygen consumption, with the effect concentrated on Complex I–dependent respiration; propofol exposure did not produce the same suppression. That distinction is the clinically actionable part — it's a volatile-agent-specific vulnerability, not a blanket anesthesia risk, which is why total intravenous anesthesia is emerging as the primary risk-mitigation strategy for patients on the affected differential, rather than avoiding anesthesia altogether. A companion measure, S 2111, is moving in the Senate. Rhode Island would join the majority of states that have already dropped mandatory physician oversight of CRNA practice if either bill reaches the governor's desk. Rhode Island General Assembly · 2026 — H 7426 The National Scorecard: Where Supervision Opt-Outs and Independent Practice Stand Now As of this year, 25 states plus Guam have formally opted out of the federal Medicare requirement that a physician supervise CRNA-administered anesthesia, while 29 states plus Washington, D.C. now permit CRNAs to practice without physician supervision under their own nurse practice acts — two related but legally distinct tallies that are easy to conflate. The opt-out count governs Medicare billing; the practice-act count governs what a CRNA may actually do day to day, and individual facility policy can still impose supervision requirements even where state law doesn't require it. Confirm against your own pharmacy's supply before assuming availability. 💡 Knowledge Pearl Recognizing and treating Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) when a block goes wrong. LAST results from unintentional intravascular injection or excessive systemic absorption of local anesthetic, producing a spectrum from perioral numbness and tinnitus to seizures and, in the most severe cases, cardiovascular collapse. Cardiac arrest can be the presenting sign with bupivacaine specifically, because its high protein binding and lipophilicity let it linger in cardiac tissue and block sodium channels longer than lidocaine does. CNS warning signs may be masked entirely under general anesthesia or heavy sedation, so cardiovascular instability out of proportion to the clinical picture should raise suspicion for LAST on its own. Treatment starts with stopping the injection, calling for help, and securing the airway with 100% oxygen — preventing the acidosis and hypoxia that worsen toxicity — followed immediately by 20% lipid emulsion: a 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then a continuous infusion, per the current ASRA checklist. Avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, and beta blockers, which ASRA's guideline flags as harmful in this setting, and be prepared for a prolonged resuscitation — LAST-related cardiac arrest can require chest compressions well past the usual ACLS endpoints while the lipid emulsion takes effect. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History August 9, 1819 William Thomas Green Morton, the Boston dentist who gave the world its first successful public demonstration of surgical anesthesia, was born in Charlton, Massachusetts. Twenty-seven years later, on October 16, 1846, Morton administered ether to patient Edward Gilbert Abbott in the Bulfinch Building amphitheater at Massachusetts General Hospital — now nicknamed the "Ether Dome" — while surgeon John Collins Warren removed a vascular tumor from Abbott's neck. Warren's reported remark to the assembled crowd, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug," marked the moment surgical pain stopped being an unavoidable cost of survival. Morton spent much of his later life in patent disputes over the discovery — he'd tried to market ether anesthesia commercially under the name "Letheon" — and died largely impoverished in 1868, but the October demonstration remains the date the profession marks as anesthesia's public birth, with Morton's August birthday a quieter footnote in the same story. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A 34-year-old man with a T6 spinal cord injury sustained three weeks ago presents for incision and drainage of a sacral abscess. The surgeon requests rapid-sequence induction. Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agent choices is most appropriate, and why? A Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg — its rapid onset and short duration make it ideal for RSI regardless of injury timeline B Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg — succinylcholine can produce life-threatening hyperkalemia beginning roughly 24–72 hours after a denervation injury and persisting for 6–9 months or longer C Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg — it's safe here because the injury is spinal cord, not peripheral nerve D Cisatracurium 0.15 mg/kg — it has the fastest onset of any non-depolarizing agent, matching succinylcholine's speed without the risk Correct answer: B — High-dose rocuronium matches succinylcholine's speed without the hyperkalemia risk Denervation injuries — spinal cord injury, burns, prolonged immobility, stroke, Guillain-Barré syndrome — trigger proliferation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors across the affected muscle membrane. Succinylcholine's depolarization of that expanded receptor field can release enough potassium to cause cardiac arrest, with risk beginning around 24–72 hours post-injury and persisting for many months until the receptor upregulation resolves. Rocuronium at 1.2 mg/kg achieves an onset (roughly 60 seconds) comparable to succinylcholine, making it the standard substitute for RSI in this population. C is wrong because spinal cord injury produces the same extrajunctional receptor proliferation below the level of injury as peripheral denervation does — the risk isn't limited to peripheral nerve damage. D's premise is simply false: rocuronium, not cisatracurium, is the fastest-onset non-depolarizing agent, which is exactly why rocuronium — not cisatracurium — is the go-to RSI substitute when succinylcholine is contraindicated. The Ether Gazette — July 27, 2026 ☰ ☀ The Ether Gazette Archive & Search Browse the Archive A Weekly Dispatch for the Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist The Ether Gazette “Vigilance, distilled.” Week of July 27, 2026 Vol. 1, No. 5 Est. 2026 📰 Headlines FDA Investigates Sevoflurane After Reports of Fatal Neurologic Complications Tied to a Rare Genetic Variant On July 2, the FDA alerted clinicians that it is investigating sevoflurane and other volatile anesthetics following published reports of "unexpected catastrophic outcomes" — severe neurologic injury and death — in adult and pediatric patients of maternal Venezuelan ancestry after routine general anesthesia. A rare mitochondrial variant, MT-ND4 m.11232T>C, has turned up in a subset of the affected patients, and the agency notes the concern could extend to volatile anesthetics as a class, not sevoflurane alone. The alert follows a joint ASA/Society for Pediatric Anesthesia notice issued January 27 flagging the same pattern. For now, the FDA advises clinicians caring for patients of Venezuelan maternal lineage to consider intravenous or regional techniques over volatile agents where clinically appropriate, and to report suspected cases through MedWatch. FDA · FDA Alerts Health Care Providers to Cases of Neurologic Complications from General Anesthesia Linked to Genetic Variant More Than 80% of Surgery Centers Now Plan to Staff Anesthesia Through Contractors, Not Employees A new Becker's ASC survey of ambulatory surgery center leaders finds independent-contractor arrangements — 44% with a stipend, 36% without — have become the dominant anesthesia staffing model for 2026, together outpacing traditional direct-employment coverage, which only 9% of leaders still expect to use. Leaders point to deepening workforce shortages, rising compensation demands, and reimbursement that hasn't kept pace, forcing many centers to subsidize coverage that used to be cost-neutral. The same survey finds ASCs increasingly leaning on CRNA-only and hybrid care-team models to keep rooms running, with certified anesthesiologist assistants picking up a growing share of that work as more states open CAA practice pathways. Menino Convention & Exhibition Center, a short walk from the Ether Dome at Massachusetts General Hospital where William T.G. Morton demonstrated ether anesthesia in October 1846. Registration details → 📚 From the Literature A Nerve Block Before Hip Fracture Surgery May Protect the Heart, Not Just Control Pain A two-center retrospective cohort study of 1,467 older adults with high cardiac risk undergoing hip fracture surgery found that adding a single-injection peripheral nerve block to general or neuraxial anesthesia was associated with a lower rate of postoperative myocardial injury than anesthesia without a block. The authors' leading explanation isn't purely analgesic: uncontrolled pain drives sympathetic activation and higher cardiac workload, so better pain control from the block may blunt the physiologic stress that leads to perioperative myocardial injury (MINS) in a population that often can't tolerate it. For students, it's a useful nudge to think of regional techniques as cardiac risk mitigation, not just an opioid-sparing add-on — particularly in exactly the frail, high-risk population hip fracture patients represent. As a retrospective cohort study, it shows association, not proof of causation; a prospective trial would be needed to confirm the effect. The law is explicitly declarative rather than expansive: it doesn't broaden what CRNAs may do, but it closes ambiguity that had left California's anesthesia-services framework resting mostly on a 2012 appellate decision rather than statute. Confirm against your own pharmacy's supply before assuming availability. 💡 Knowledge Pearl Why an unmasked mitochondrial disorder can turn a routine general anesthetic catastrophic. This week's FDA alert on sevoflurane is a sharp reminder that volatile anesthetics aren't metabolically inert. Mitochondria generate the ATP that excitable, oxygen-hungry tissue — brain and heart chief among it — depends on minute to minute, and volatile agents are known to mildly suppress mitochondrial electron transport chain activity as part of how they produce anesthesia. In a patient with a normal mitochondrial reserve, that suppression is trivial and fully reversible. In a patient carrying a pathogenic mitochondrial variant — like the MT-ND4 m.11232T>C mutation implicated in the current cases — baseline oxidative capacity is already reduced, and volatile-agent suppression on top of that can tip vulnerable tissue into energy failure, producing exactly the picture being reported: unexplained neurologic devastation or cardiac collapse in patients with no other risk factors. The practical takeaway for boards and bedside alike isn't "avoid volatiles in everyone" — it's recognizing when mitochondrial disease is on the differential (unexplained lactic acidosis, myopathy, prior anesthetic complications, suggestive family or ancestry history) and defaulting toward total intravenous or regional techniques in those patients, since propofol and regional anesthesia don't carry the same electron-transport-chain liability at clinical doses. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 25, 1894 Harold Griffith was born in Montreal on this date — the anesthetist who, on January 23, 1942, gave the world its first practical neuromuscular blocking agent. Working with resident Enid Johnson at the Homeopathic Hospital of Montreal, Griffith injected an extract of curare, Intocostrin , into a 20-year-old undergoing an appendectomy, producing profound muscle relaxation without deepening the ether anesthesia already in progress. Before that afternoon, adequate relaxation for abdominal surgery meant anesthetizing patients dangerously deep; Griffith's report, published later that year, opened the door to lighter, safer anesthesia paired with deliberate paralysis — the conceptual split between hypnosis, analgesia, and relaxation that still organizes how anesthesia is taught today. Griffith went on to introduce cyclopropane to Canadian practice, establish the country's first postoperative recovery room, and serve as founding president of the World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists. 🧠 Board Question of the Week In the PACU, a patient extubated 20 minutes ago after a laparoscopic case involving rocuronium develops intermittent upper-airway obstruction, uncoordinated jerky limb movements, and difficulty maintaining a sustained head lift. A qualitative peripheral nerve stimulator shows a train-of-four with no fade appreciable to the observer. Which statement best describes this scenario? A Residual neuromuscular blockade has been definitively ruled out because the train-of-four shows no fade B Clinically significant residual blockade can still be present; qualitative train-of-four monitoring reliably detects fade only once the train-of-four ratio has fallen below about 0.4, well short of the 0.9 threshold associated with these symptoms C These findings are more consistent with emergence delirium than with neuromuscular blockade D A normal train-of-four by any method excludes residual paralysis as a cause of postoperative airway obstruction Correct answer: B — Qualitative TOF can look reassuring while real residual blockade persists The vignette describes classic signs of residual neuromuscular blockade: upper-airway obstruction, uncoordinated movement, and inability to sustain a head lift — a bedside surrogate for a train-of-four ratio below roughly 0.9, the threshold below which pharyngeal function and airway protection are impaired. The trap in this question is the "normal" qualitative TOF: the human eye reliably detects fade only when the train-of-four ratio has already dropped well below 0.4, so a qualitative twitch monitor can look unremarkable at ratios between roughly 0.4 and 0.9 — precisely the range where clinically meaningful residual paralysis lives. This gap is the rationale behind APSF's ongoing push for quantitative neuromuscular monitoring (which reports an actual numeric TOF ratio) as the more reliable standard before extubation. Emergence delirium doesn't produce upper-airway obstruction or an inability to sustain a head lift as its primary features, so C is a weaker fit for this clinical picture. D repeats the same qualitative-versus-quantitative trap as A — a "normal" TOF by qualitative assessment never fully excludes clinically important residual blockade, whereas a quantitative TOF ratio at or above 0.9 does. A Weekly Dispatch for the Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist The Ether Gazette “Vigilance, distilled.” Week of July 20, 2026 Vol. 1, No. 4 Est. 2026 📰 Headlines Ohio Tells CMS It No Longer Needs the Federal Physician-Supervision Rule for CRNAs On July 10, Governor Mike DeWine notified the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services that Ohio is opting out of the federal requirement that a physician supervise CRNA-administered anesthesia, writing that the mandate "is no longer needed" given the state's newly modernized nurse-anesthesia law. The certification follows House Bill 52, which DeWine signed in March and which took effect June 8, replacing Ohio's decades-old supervision language with a collaborative-practice model built around current CRNA training and standards. CMS has allowed governors to make this certification since 2001, and a growing roster of states has done so since — though, as always, opting out of the federal Medicare condition is a separate question from what each state's own nurse practice act permits. Yahoo Finance · Ohio Opts Out of Physician Supervision for CRNAs A Widening Gap: Report Projects the U.S. Will Be Short 12,500 CRNAs by 2033 A workforce analysis making the rounds this month puts hard numbers on a familiar strain: the U.S. is on pace to be short roughly 12,500 CRNAs by 2033 — nearly 22 percent of today's workforce — as retirements accelerate faster than training programs can replace them. About 31 percent of practicing CRNAs are already 55 or older, while the nation's 155 accredited programs graduate only around 2,400 new CRNAs a year, barely enough to offset departures, let alone grow the pipeline. Rural facilities, which lean most heavily on CRNAs for anesthesia coverage, are expected to feel the shortfall first and hardest. Becker's ASC · The Anesthesia Workforce Shortage Demystified NorthStar's CEO and Chief Anesthetist Officer Talk Private Equity and the Next Decade of Anesthesia In AANA's "State of Anesthesia: 2026" conversation, NorthStar Anesthesia CEO Adam Spiegel and Chief Anesthetist Officer Randy Moore, DNP, MBA, CRNA — who spent four years as AANA's own CEO before joining NorthStar — walked through what's reshaping the business of anesthesia: a tightening CRNA labor market, shifting hospital-employment dynamics, and the growing footprint of private equity in anesthesia staffing groups. The pair expanded on the same themes at this year's Annual Congress in a session titled "Anesthesia 2030: Business Models, Workforce Shifts, and the Future of Practice" — worth a look for anyone trying to read where employment models are headed before they graduate into one. Registration details → 📚 From the Literature Bigger Trial, Same Old Answer: Propofol Doesn't Beat Volatile Anesthesia on Cancer Survival The long-awaited GA-CARES trial — a pragmatic, five-center randomized trial testing whether propofol-based total intravenous anesthesia improves survival after resection of high-risk cancers (pancreas, esophagus, lung, stomach, bile duct, liver, bladder, or peritoneal surface) compared with volatile-agent maintenance — reported its results this year. The answer was no: two-year mortality ran slightly higher in the propofol arm (26.1%) than the volatile arm (22.9%), and the trial did not support the retrospective-data-driven hypothesis that propofol's anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties translate into a survival benefit. For students who've absorbed a decade of buzz about propofol's theoretical oncologic edge, GA-CARES is a useful corrective: choose your maintenance agent on hemodynamics, PONV risk, and clinical context — not on an unproven cancer-outcomes argument. After the comment period closed on October 25, opposition led by LifeLinc Anesthesia argued the rule conflicted with the state's own Nursing Practice Act, that 92 percent of surveyed rural surgeons said they'd refuse the new responsibilities outright, and that compliance could cost individual facilities $800,000 to $1.2 million a year — money many rural hospitals don't have. The Board withdrew the proposal, preserving Mississippi's existing collaborative-care model, at least for now. Confirm against your own pharmacy's supply before assuming availability. 💡 Knowledge Pearl Why 20% lipid emulsion reverses local anesthetic cardiotoxicity. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) starts with CNS signs — perioral numbness, tinnitus, a metallic taste, agitation — and can progress within minutes to seizures and, in the worst cases, cardiovascular collapse that's notoriously resistant to standard ACLS. Bupivacaine is the classic villain: highly lipophilic and tightly protein-bound, it partitions into cardiac tissue and blocks myocardial sodium channels longer and more potently than less lipophilic agents like lidocaine or ropivacaine. The fix is almost as counterintuitive as the injury: 20% IV lipid emulsion, given as a 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by a 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion. The leading explanation is the "lipid sink" — an expanded intravascular lipid phase that pulls lipophilic local anesthetic molecules out of cardiac tissue and plasma faster than they can act — alongside a proposed direct metabolic and inotropic effect on stressed myocardium. Per ASRA's LAST checklist, propofol is not an acceptable substitute for lipid emulsion (its lipid content is too low and its cardiodepressant effects work against you), and standard resuscitation doses of epinephrine should be reduced, since large boluses appear to worsen outcomes in LAST-associated arrest. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 25, 1834 On this date, the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge died in London at 61 — best remembered for "Kubla Khan" and "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner," but also, decades earlier, an eager volunteer in one of anesthesia's true prehistory experiments. In 1799, Coleridge was among the writers and thinkers who gathered at Thomas Beddoes's Pneumatic Institution in Bristol to inhale a curious new gas prepared by a young lab assistant named Humphry Davy: nitrous oxide. Coleridge described a sensation of "highly pleasurable thrilling" throughout his limbs, and Davy — who nearly injured himself testing gases on his own body throughout the project — went on to note, almost as an aside in his 1800 research volume, that nitrous oxide "appears capable of destroying physical pain" and might be used "with advantage during surgical operations." Forty-seven years would pass before anyone acted on that observation. 🧠 Board Question of the Week During an ultrasound-guided interscalene block, a patient becomes agitated and reports a metallic taste and ringing in her ears about 60 seconds after the local anesthetic is injected. Before the block needle is even withdrawn, she has a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. After securing the airway and terminating the seizure, which intervention should be initiated next? A A therapeutic dose of intravenous propofol to provide ongoing sedation B 20% intravenous lipid emulsion, 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by a continuous infusion C A full resuscitation dose of intravenous epinephrine per standard ACLS dosing D Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize the cardiac membrane Correct answer: B — 20% intravenous lipid emulsion This presentation — early neurologic symptoms rapidly progressing to seizure right after a large-volume peripheral nerve block — is textbook local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), most likely from inadvertent intravascular injection or rapid systemic absorption. ASRA's LAST checklist calls for airway management, seizure suppression with a benzodiazepine, and 20% lipid emulsion as first-line treatment: a 1.5 mL/kg bolus (roughly 100 mL in an average adult), repeatable up to twice for persistent cardiovascular collapse, followed by an infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min until hemodynamic stability is restored. Propofol is specifically discouraged as a lipid-emulsion substitute — its lipid concentration is too low to produce a meaningful sink effect, and its cardiodepressant properties can worsen an already unstable patient. Standard ACLS epinephrine doses should be reduced (to boluses of ≤1 mcg/kg) rather than given at full resuscitation doses, since case and animal data suggest large doses impair resuscitation from LAST-associated arrest. Calcium has no established role in LAST management; it treats hyperkalemia and calcium-channel-blocker toxicity, not local anesthetic cardiotoxicity. Unlike midazolam, which depends on hepatic CYP3A4, remimazolam is broken down by tissue esterases — the same organ-independent pathway that makes remifentanil so predictable. The result is rapid, consistent offset that doesn't accumulate in hepatic or renal impairment, and a context-sensitive half-time that barely rises with infusion duration. It's still a benzodiazepine at its core: it binds the GABA-A receptor and is fully reversible with flumazenil, which is more than can be said for propofol. That combination — organ-independent clearance plus a rescue reversal agent — is why remimazolam keeps showing up in board questions about induction choices in the hemodynamically fragile patient. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 15, 1868 William T. G. Morton, the Boston dentist who administered the first publicly demonstrated surgical ether anesthetic at Massachusetts General Hospital on October 16, 1846, died on this date — reportedly after collapsing during a carriage ride through New York's Central Park, having spent much of his later life in a bitter and financially ruinous fight over credit for the discovery. He never secured the recognition — or the patent royalties — he spent two decades pursuing; today the amphitheater where he administered that first ether anesthetic is preserved as the "Ether Dome," a National Historic Landmark. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A patient receives succinylcholine for rapid-sequence induction and remains apneic and unable to breathe spontaneously 90 minutes after a single intubating dose, with no other identifiable cause. A dibucaine number of 22 is subsequently reported. What does this finding indicate? A Normal pseudocholinesterase activity; the prolonged block is unrelated to enzyme function B Heterozygous atypical pseudocholinesterase, with roughly 50% normal enzyme activity C Homozygous atypical pseudocholinesterase, with markedly reduced ability to hydrolyze succinylcholine D Pseudocholinesterase inhibition from a drug interaction, unrelated to genotype Correct answer: C — Homozygous atypical pseudocholinesterase The dibucaine number reflects the percentage inhibition of pseudocholinesterase activity by dibucaine, not enzyme quantity or concentration. A normal homozygous genotype yields a dibucaine number around 70–80; heterozygotes typically fall in the 40–60 range with moderately prolonged block (20–30 minutes); homozygous atypical individuals score roughly 20 or below and can remain paralyzed for hours, since their enzyme binds dibucaine — and succinylcholine — poorly. Management is supportive: sedation, continued mechanical ventilation, and reassurance that the block will resolve as succinylcholine is slowly hydrolyzed by non-specific esterases elsewhere in the body. Reversal agents have no role here, since there is no acetylcholinesterase-mediated neuromuscular blockade to reverse. MH is triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine in genetically susceptible patients (most often via RYR1 mutations), causing the ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum to dump calcium into the muscle cytoplasm uncontrollably. That flood of calcium drives sustained contraction, runaway heat production, and skyrocketing oxygen consumption — the hypermetabolic state that produces the classic triad of rising end-tidal CO2, muscle rigidity, and fever. Dantrolene binds the RYR1 receptor directly and blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, cutting off the process at its source rather than just treating the downstream fever or acidosis. Initial dosing is 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated every 5–10 minutes until symptoms resolve — there is no fixed maximum in an ongoing crisis. Because a single reaction doesn't fully rule a patient out or in, current guidance leans on a short screening history (personal or family MH reaction, and any prior genetic testing) to decide who actually needs formal RYR1 / CACNA1S / STAC3 sequencing, rather than testing everyone with a vague family rumor of "anesthesia problems." 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History June 17, 1931 On June 17, 1931, Agatha Hodgins founded the National Association of Nurse Anesthetists — the organization that would become today's AANA — in Cleveland, Ohio. Hodgins, who had already helped establish nurse anesthesia training at Lakeside Hospital and co-founded the Lakeside Alumnae Association of Nurse Anesthetists a decade earlier, built the national association specifically to defend nurse anesthetists' right to practice against a wave of early-20th-century legal challenges arguing that administering anesthesia constituted the unlicensed practice of medicine. Nearly a century later, the fight over who gets to define and defend that scope of practice — see this week's Legislation Tracker — is still very much alive. 🧠 Board Question of the Week Per the ASA's 2026 practice guideline, a patient undergoing an open abdominal procedure receives a bilateral transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block as part of a multimodal analgesia plan. Which of the following best describes what this fascial plane block actually accomplishes? A It blocks visceral afferents from the abdominal organs, eliminating deep intra-abdominal pain B It blocks somatic sensory afferents (roughly T6–L1) supplying the anterior abdominal wall, reducing incisional pain and opioid need C It blocks sympathetic chain fibers, producing a spinal-like sympathectomy and blood pressure drop D It blocks phrenic nerve fibers, reducing diaphragmatic irritation from pneumoperitoneum Correct answer: B — Somatic sensory afferents of the anterior abdominal wall A TAP block deposits local anesthetic in the fascial plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, where the somatic sensory nerves supplying the anterior abdominal wall (roughly T6–L1) travel. It reliably reduces incisional (somatic) pain and opioid consumption in the first 24 postoperative hours — exactly the outcome the 2026 ASA guideline's "strong" recommendation is based on — but it does not touch visceral pain from the bowel, peritoneum, or other organs, which travels via separate autonomic pathways. A is wrong because visceral afferents aren't in the TAP plane at all, which is why patients still need systemic multimodal analgesia for deep visceral discomfort. C describes neuraxial (spinal/epidural) sympathetic blockade, not a peripheral fascial plane block. D is incorrect — the phrenic nerve runs nowhere near the TAP plane; diaphragmatic irritation from pneumoperitoneum isn't addressed by this block. Unlike neostigmine, which reverses neuromuscular blockade indirectly by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and raising synaptic acetylcholine, sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that forms a tight 1:1 host-guest complex directly around the steroidal neuromuscular blocker molecule in the plasma. This encapsulation creates a concentration gradient that pulls free rocuronium or vecuronium off nicotinic receptors and out of the neuromuscular junction, back into plasma for renal clearance as an inactive complex. The practical payoff: sugammadex can reverse even profound (deep) blockade reliably, works faster than neostigmine at comparable depths, and — because it doesn't act on acetylcholinesterase — carries none of neostigmine's muscarinic side effects (bradycardia, bronchospasm, secretions), so it doesn't require co-administration with an antimuscarinic like glycopyrrolate. It has no reversal activity against benzylisoquinolinium blockers (e.g., cisatracurium) or succinylcholine, since those aren't steroidal molecules it can encapsulate. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 1940 In July 1940, the American Society of Anesthesiologists published the first issue of Anesthesiology , under founding editor-in-chief Henry S. Ruth, MD. It was a deliberate act of professionalization: anesthesia had only recently begun separating from surgery as its own discipline, and a dedicated, peer-reviewed journal gave the young specialty a place to build a real evidence base rather than passing technique down purely by apprenticeship. Eight and a half decades later, Anesthesiology remains the field's flagship journal — including, this month, the very 2026 practice guideline covered above. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A patient receiving a ropivacaine infusion for a continuous interscalene nerve block develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, and then a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure 20 minutes after catheter bolus dosing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management, assuming the airway is secured and seizure activity is controlled? A Administer high-dose epinephrine (1 mg IV) per standard ACLS arrest dosing B Give a second local anesthetic bolus through the catheter to "burn off" the receptor C Begin 20% lipid emulsion therapy (bolus followed by continuous infusion) D Administer flumazenil to reverse the neurologic toxicity Correct answer: C — Begin 20% lipid emulsion therapy This presentation is classic local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST): early CNS signs (perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste) progressing to seizure, which can precede cardiovascular collapse. Per ASRA's LAST checklist, once the airway/seizure is managed, first-line treatment is 20% lipid emulsion — typically a 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 2–3 minutes followed by a 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion — which acts as a "lipid sink," partitioning lipophilic local anesthetic away from cardiac and neural tissue. A is wrong because ACLS-dose epinephrine (versus the reduced <1 mcg/kg boluses ASRA recommends in LAST) can worsen arrhythmias and impair lipid resuscitation. B is wrong and dangerous — more local anesthetic deepens toxicity. D treats benzodiazepine toxicity, not LAST, and doesn't address the underlying problem.
